gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a measured number. ServeTheHome measured the $89.99 ASUS ZenScreen MB169CK, the portable monitor ChatGPT itself showed, at a peak of 140.2 nits and 68% sRGB, which is dimmer than the 185 cd/m² centre reading Notebookcheck measured on a FOPO triple laptop screen extender. Even so, Notebookcheck said it would 'likely go with the individual portable monitors' over that extender, because of the extender's build, not its screen.
standout_why: I compared against the three cited pages. bestbuy.ca's article body did not come through (fetched 2026-11-21). What did come through was product tiles with CAD prices and customer snippets, and no measurements. bestusefultips.com has no figures at all: no nits, watts or weights, and no named reviewer. ViewSonic's blog gives only ViewSonic's own specs for the VG1457 (2.6 lb, 65 W PD), with no outside testing. ChatGPT's two answers say extenders are 'often average' for screen quality and that portable monitors have 'more high-quality options', but neither puts a number on either category. I did not open the uncited TechRadar best-portable-monitor page, so I can't say whether it has numbers.
decides: It backs the overall pick of a portable monitor for most shoppers. The reason is the build: Notebookcheck found the FOPO extender's hinges 'tend to teeter', the plastic twists and creaks, and the unit 'works best if you only intend to set it up once'. It does not back ChatGPT's reason. At the budget end, the portable monitor ChatGPT showed measured dimmer (140.2 nits) and with less colour (68% sRGB) than the measured extender (185 cd/m² centre, 79% sRGB). The extender's real screen weakness is contrast: 247:1 against the MB169CK's 980:1 at full brightness. So the page should say screen quality depends on the panel, not on whether it's an extender or a portable monitor, and that the deciding issues are build or hinge load and the video path.

findings.label: Brightness, measured
findings.value: 185 cd/m² centre; 193.1 cd/m² max; 177.4 cd/m² average; 85% uniformity
findings.source_title: FOPO 12-inch triple monitor extender review: Clunky and more fragile than standalone portable monitors (Notebookcheck)
findings.note: Allen Ngo, Notebookcheck, published 2022-07-23. Tested on a 2022 HP Pavilion Plus 14 and measured as one grid across the unit, not panel by panel. The page lists the minimum as 17.77 cd/m², which doesn't fit the grid and looks like a typo, so I left it out. This is an older 12-inch FOPO, not the S1/S7/S10/S11/S788 we link.

findings.label: Contrast, black level and colour gamut, measured
findings.value: 247:1 contrast; black level 0.75 cd/m²; 79% sRGB, 79% AdobeRGB, 77.1% Display P3; ColorChecker DeltaE 4.59 (0.84 after calibration)
findings.note: Notebookcheck's Calman results. Response time was 29.2 ms black/white and 31.6 ms grey 50/80%. No PWM at any brightness.

findings.label: Notebookcheck verdict, extender vs standalone portable monitors
findings.value: "we would likely go with the individual portable monitors"
findings.note: Allen Ngo also says the hinges 'tend to teeter more than we would like' and that the mostly plastic build twists and creaks. He recommends the rear kickstand to avoid straining the laptop's hinges, and says it 'works best if you only intend to set it up once'. Windows saw the two side screens as 'two ordinary external monitors'. The review does not measure weight or power.

findings.note: Sam Sabinash, ServeTheHome, published 2026-07-12, measured with a Datacolor SpyderPro. This is the standalone portable monitor ChatGPT showed at $89.99 in the first chat.

findings.label: Contrast, colour gamut and accuracy, measured
findings.value: Contrast 610:1 at minimum brightness, a peak of 1110:1 at 50%, and 980:1 at maximum; 68% sRGB, 51% AdobeRGB, 50% P3; DeltaE average 3.74 (min 0.74, max 12.42)
findings.note: Datacolor SpyderPro. Put side by side with Notebookcheck's FOPO figures: the MB169CK has about 4x the contrast (980:1 vs 247:1) but less brightness (140.2 vs 185 cd/m²) and less sRGB coverage (68% vs 79%). The two outlets used different instruments and the tests were years apart.

findings.note: Measured on USB-C input. This is the drain on a laptop's battery for one bus-powered 15.6-inch screen.
